reception.text: The Morning Oregonian gave the November Idaho reserves a stacked page-2 headline, putting four new reserves at 7,406,556 acres and reading the result as the administration brushing aside Senator Weldon B. Heyburn's protests.
California papers reported the year's proclamations as local news; a search for 1906 returned 24 items and no fight like the one in Idaho.
Utah papers reported the proclamations as news from Washington or the land office; searches returned 82 items on proclamations and 47 on protests, none of them against a 1906 proclamation.

political_impact.text: The Forest Service answered the charge that land was being locked up by saying the reserves' resources would remain open to use and development, with cutting limited to mature timber.
A Washington dispatch linked the November 5–7 burst of twenty-eight proclamations to Roosevelt's departure for Panama rather than to the election on November 6.

Western stockmen, timbermen and their senators increasingly denounced the reserves as a federal lock-up of land beyond the reach of states and settlers, and grazing fees as a tax Congress had never voted.

legacy.text: In February 1907 Congress barred new forest reserves and additions to existing ones in Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Colorado and Wyoming except by act of Congress, and renamed the reserves national forests.

A wave of consolidations in July 1908 folded many of the smaller 1906 reserves into larger forests, and boundaries have shifted many times since, so no single 1906 proclamation maps neatly onto one modern forest.
